adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's country overview (LGBTQ rights in Indonesia) sets out the national framework a visitor to North Kalimantan stands under: Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections based on sexual orientation or gender identity, legal gender recognition requires sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval, and same-sex marriage is not recognised. The page records that the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sex outside marriage - in force from 2 January 2026 - carries up to one year in prison, that homosexuality is illegal in Aceh under Sharia law (flogging or imprisonment), and that a proposed obscenity article explicitly naming 'same sex' is feared to trigger discriminatory regional bylaws - the provincial-regulation mechanism the record's own analysis flags. It also logs Indonesia's votes against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, a 2025 Pew figure of 93% of Indonesians calling homosexuality 'morally unacceptable', and conversion therapy widely practised and openly advertised. This is the operative framework behind the record's at-national-score assessment, documented with dates, figures and outcomes.

adds.title: Vitaly Milonov - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's biography of Vitaly Milonov documents the city-level origin of the anti-LGBT law a trans visitor to Saint Petersburg stands under: as a member of the Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly (2007-2016) he is recorded as the principal sponsor of the legislation criminalising 'homosexual propaganda directed toward minors' - the city ban enacted in 2012 that the cited New York Times report 'Anti-Gay Law Stirs Fears in Russia' (29 February 2012) covered, with the page quoting his statement that he fully intended to catch Madonna committing a possible offence under it when the pop diva visited the city. The page also records Milonov stating in 2013 that gay athletes could be arrested at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics if they promoted homosexuality to minors, and his protests against the city's Side by Side LGBT film festival in November 2013. This is the most jurisdiction-specific enforcement origin available for the record's local assessment of LGBT-hostile measures in the city.

adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Russia - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's country overview (LGBTQ rights in Russia) supplies the federal framework Saint Petersburg is assessed under: a 2013 law criminalises distributing 'propaganda' of 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors, with fines up to 5,000 roubles for citizens, 50,000 for officials, and 1 million roubles plus up to 90 days' suspension for organisations, while foreigners face up to 15 days' detention, a fine up to 100,000 roubles and deportation. The page records that ten regions including Saint Petersburg (2012) enacted regional versions of the ban before the federal law, and that Saint Petersburg removed its regional law in 2014, leaving the federal statute in force there. It also notes a July 2023 law banning gender transition outright - prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition - and a 2010 European Court of Human Rights ruling fining Russia over the systematic refusal of pride-event permits. This grounds the record's national-score anchor with dated, sourced specifics.
